## Abstract

::: {.abstract}
During COVID-19 I communicated model outputs to three audiences.
Government, through weekly estimates and reports to the UK's scientific
advisory groups and the consensus statements they produced.
The public, through a dashboard of reproduction number estimates that ran
from 2020 to 2022 and sometimes published estimates that made no sense.
Other scientists, through forecast hubs, where a forecast becomes part of
an ensemble and can be hard to learn from.
I say what worked for each and what I would do differently.

The software we built was a fourth channel.
A package default is a decision the user inherits.
The limits of a method travel less well than the method.
The epinowcast community and our forecast evaluation tools were attempts to
communicate through software and the people around it.

The second half asks what changes when both the writer and the reader have
a language model.
I describe how I use coding agents, how I make that visible with a bot
account and a published prompt log, and what checking their output has
taught me.
Under AI, prose starts to sound the same and it gets harder to say who is
accountable for a number.
The failure mode is confident, plausible, wrong.
I end with what I would like us to agree on.
:::

The organisers asked for a communication-focused lecture of about 30
minutes, tentatively titled *Science Communication with and under AI*, as
a starting point to make my own.
They suggested my experience during COVID-19 with government bodies, the
public and fellow scientists, including building widely used R packages for
the modelling community, as the material.
